To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) task engagement is dynamically controlled by strategic processes that can be manipulated experimentally and 2) increased task engagement attenuates the detrimental effect of auditory distraction by reducing the processing of distractors at encoding, thereby reducing the likelihood that they come to mind at test.

the detrimental effects of auditory distraction are attenuated by an increase in task engagement, and that this effect is due to the reduction of the encoding of the distracting information, which prevents it from coming to mind during retrieval.

the detrimental effect of irrelevant speech on memory is attenuated when the task is more engaging, and that this attenuation is due to the fact that the task engages a more effective cognitive control system that is capable of suppressing the processing of irrelevant speech.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the mechanisms that allow us to filter out irrelevant information from the sensory input.
how we can use our cognitive control abilities to shield against auditory distractions, and we have found that we can use cognitive control to shield against distractions at encoding.
how we control the processing of distracting information in our environment, in particular, how we control the distracting effects of irrelevant sounds.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the present study provides evidence that the cognitive control of irrelevant auditory information is a dynamic process that can be adjusted in a flexible and strategic manner.
the results show that the cognitive control of irrelevant sounds can be modulated dynamically and that the cognitive engagement in the task can be modulated strategically.

task engagement is dynamically controlled and can be modulate to shield against auditory distractions by attenuating distractors processing at encoding and preventing distractors from entering the mind at test.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the detrimental effects of irrelevant speech on recall of visually presented words is attenuated under conditions of reduced target-word discriminablity (i.e., increased task engagement).

we have demonstrated that dynamic control of the detrimental effect of irrelevant auditory information can occur through a reduction in the encoding of the irrelevant information, and that this can be accomplished through a reduction of task engagement.

the detrimental effects of irrelevant sound can be reduced by increasing the task engagement of the focal task, and the mechanism by which this occurs is through the reduction of the encoding of the irrelevant sound.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we can control how much we are distracted by irrelevant sounds.
the detrimental effect of auditory distraction on cognitive performance is not inevitable.
people can dynamically adjust the amount of cognitive control they exert to deal with distracting sounds.
